tier_reason: results/fastest.json has sorting rows against std::sort (run 2026-09-04-algorithms: gcc 13.3.0, -O3 -march=native -std=c++23, 'Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz' 4 cores), produced by bench/bench_sort.cpp. Compiler, flags and CPU are stated, but the repo is private so the benchmark code is not public, which rules out A. There is no paper or independent third-party suite, so it cannot be B. That leaves first-party numbers: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: vs std::sort on 1M int64 (results/fastest.json rows, run 2026-09-04-algorithms): 6.63x already-sorted (1.418ms vs 9.403ms), 3.42x few-unique/8 values (6.147ms vs 20.996ms), 2.28x random (24.567ms vs 56.106ms). LOSES 0.93x on almost-sorted/1% swapped (derived from page data: 12.471ms vs 11.640ms; the page records this as std::sort winning 1.07x, 'about 7-10% across runs'). The other three patterns are not in fastest.json. Their exact values come from the message of commit 2fa7d3d, and README.md rounds them: 2.33x sorted+1% appended (README 2.3x), 1.71x sawtooth (README 1.7x), 1.55x reverse-sorted (README 1.6x; the fastest.json note gives 1.55-1.93x after the pivot fix). A pivot-arrangement fix is an internal before/after comparison, not against std::sort: 2.86x on 1M reverse-sorted (3.803ms vs 10.864ms); before the fix fastcpp was 0.55x vs std::sort. radix_sort vs std::sort on random uint64: peaks at 4.30x at n=16,384 (148.5us vs 638.6us) and drops to 2.06x at n=4,194,304, where fastcpp::algo::sort (140.5ms) beats radix (158.2ms). It LOSES around and below the n~1024 crossover (0.92x at n=1024, 0.23x at n=64).
corrections.caveats: Developer source is a PRIVATE repo (private:developer-source, 0 stars, 0 forks), readable only via authenticated `gh api`. Private code is not 'public', so this is capped below tier A even though results/fastest.json's run metadata states the compiler, flags and CPU (verified against bench/bench_sort.cpp, root CMakeLists.txt fastcpp_bench_opt/-O3 and the 'release' preset with FASTCPP_NATIVE_ARCH=ON). The CPU string names no SKU (only 'Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz'). The estimator is the minimum of 3 samples with a 50ms budget each. The run is labelled commit '7db44c2 + sorting', i.e. it was measured on a working tree before sorting commit 2fa7d3d. The 2.86x pivot-arrangement figure is a before/after measurement: the committed bench/bench_sort.cpp times only std::sort vs fastcpp::algo::sort vs radix_sort, so the old arrangement cannot be re-run from the repo. The sawtooth, reverse-sorted and appended ratios are not in results/fastest.json; they come from the commit message and README only. Only libstdc++/gcc was tested; there is no libc++ or MSVC STL comparison. The benchmark is first-party, written by the same project, and has not been independently reproduced. The repo's own results file says absolute times are not comparable across differently-timed runs on this shared cloud VM, so only within-row ratios are treated as meaningful.

notes: The main numbers check out exactly against fastest.json: 6.63/3.42/2.28/2.86/4.30 recompute from the page's ns values, and 0.93x is the inverse of the page's 1.07x std::sort win. The only precision fix is where 2.33x/1.71x/1.55x come from: the commit message and README, not benchmark_url. Metadata is confirmed via gh: MIT (spdx MIT), not a fork, not archived, private, 0 stars, last commit 2026-09-04 (active). The sort is a first-party pdqsort-style reimplementation crediting Edelkamp & Weiss BlockQuicksort; it is not a vendored copy of pdqsort.
